Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

vignette: Ahmad, a 41-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a dancer and is married, has been struggling with symptoms of PTSD following his experience in a war zone. The traumatic event occurred several years ago when he was caught in the crossfire while trying to evacuate from a city under siege. Ahmad vividly recalls the constant sound of gunfire, the pungent smell of burning rubber and soil from nearby bombings, and hearing names that reminded him of friends who were injured or killed. Since his return to the United States, these specific triggers have been potent reminders of the horror he endured. The sounds of sirens in the city or fireworks on holidays immediately transport Ahmad back to the war zone. He has also found that the smell of soil from a recent gardening project at home can trigger intense flashbacks and feelings of dread. Ahmad had come to believe that his experiences made him feel dead inside, as if he was no longer capable of experiencing joy or connection with others in the same way he did before the trauma. He felt that his faith had been shattered; he could no longer trust people or find solace in the belief systems he once held dear. The war zone experience had also left Ahmad feeling exposed and vulnerable, believing that others could easily discern what happened to him just by looking at him. This made it difficult for him to interact with colleagues and friends without constant fear of judgment and pity. As a dancer, his occupation involves performing in front of audiences, but now he often avoids public performances out of concern that the audience might be able to see the trauma etched on his face. Over time, Ahmad's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on both his personal life and career. He had grown distant from his wife, finding it increasingly difficult to share intimate moments or engage in meaningful conversations without feeling overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts and memories. His dancing performances became less frequent as he began to feel that every step reminded him of the gunfire and chaos of the war zone. The consequences of his avoidance extended beyond just his personal relationships. Ahmad's dance troupe noticed a decline in his performance quality and frequency, leading to strained professional relationships and missed opportunities for growth within the arts community. He had come to see his career as another reminder of what he could no longer escape from. What finally brought Ahmad to seek help was a series of particularly intense flashbacks during a recent rehearsal that left him unable to function properly for days afterward. The combination of auditory triggers in the rehearsal space and olfactory reminders from the outdoor setting where they often practiced had become overwhelming. He was certain that he could no longer maintain his daily life without some form of intervention. In therapy, Ahmad is most afraid of being reminded of the war zone experiences and feeling as if he will never truly recover. At the same time, he hopes to find a way to reconnect with his passions and regain faith in both himself and others. He wants to reclaim parts of his life that have been lost due to the trauma, particularly his connection to dance and those around him.
